segments.text: Ah, hello doctor. Look, it's probably nothing at all, but the missus said I should get my ankles looked at before they burst out of my socks.
Well, she sounds like a wise woman. Sit down there, Declan, and tell me what's been going on with them.
Sure, my ankles are a bit swollen, that's all. Grand otherwise. I got back from Singapore on Sunday and they've been puffy since.
Singapore! That's a fair old trip. How many hours were you in the air?
Fourteen, near enough, with a stop in Dubai. They wouldn't let me out of the seat, a wee child beside me asleep on my arm the whole way.
Ah, the worst seat in the house. So you've had the swelling since Sunday. That's about three days?
Three days, yeah. It's not sore or anything. I just notice the shoes are tight by the evening, that's all.
Tight shoes by the evening. Is it worse when you're standing about, or is it much the same all day?
Worse when I'm on my feet, definitely. And when I put my feet up on the stool at night, it goes down a good bit.
Good. Both legs, or is one worse than the other?
Ah, they're about the same, sure. I'd be wary of saying more, in case you'd start fussing.
I only fuss when people say 'it's nothing' too fast! Tell me, what do you do for work that you're flying out to Singapore?
I work in logistics. I'm the fella who makes sure the containers get on the right boat, so I'm in the air about once a month, and behind a desk the rest of the time.
A job where you sit a lot. Do you walk about at all during the day, or is it desk to car to sofa?
Desk to car to sofa, mostly, if I'm honest. I used to follow the hurling more than I played it.
Ha, the armchair seats are the best in the house. Were you drinking much water on the flight?
A couple of cups, no more. I don't like queuing for the toilet with the trolley blocking the aisle.
Very sensible reasoning, though not the best for your legs. Look, there's a good chance this is simply what long hours of sitting do. Gravity pools the fluid in the lowest part of you.
So it's just the flight, then. I thought as much.
I'm not going to say it's definitely just the flight, but nothing you've told me is alarming. Let's talk about what helps.
Go on, then. I'm all ears, though I've a call at one.
First, keep moving. A short walk every hour or so, and when you're at the desk, flex your ankles up and down under it. Are you able to do that?
I can do that. I might look daft, but nobody's looking at my feet in the office.
Second, put your feet up above hip level for a while in the evening, lying down is better than sitting on the stool.
I do that anyway when the telly's on. Grand.
Third, drink more water. And for your next flight, wear compression socks and get up for a stroll every hour or two, trolley or no trolley.
Compression socks. Oh God, a fella at work wears those, he says they're like being hugged by a boa constrictor.
Your colleague is exaggerating, I promise. They do the job of squeezing the blood back up the leg, and you'll get used to them.
All right, I'll get a pair in the chemist on the way home.

Now, one thing I do want you to hear clearly. If you notice one leg becoming much more swollen than the other, or a painful, hot calf, or any breathlessness or chest pain, don't wait, go straight to the emergency department.
A painful calf, breathlessness, chest pain. Right, I've got that. I'll tell the missus too, she'll keep me right.
Good man. Tell me, will you be able to get the socks on yourself, or will the missus be conscripted?
Ah, I'll manage. If not, I'll conscript the youngest, she'll love that.
I don't doubt it. The hope is that it settles by itself over the next week or so with the walking and the feet up.
Well, that's a relief, so it is. I'd best get back to the car before the parking warden gets me.
Off you go then. Safe travels next time, and drink the water!
I will, doctor, I will. Thanks very much now.
